derivations.claim: **Frames and local winding facts on finite disks.** Every complex bundle on a compact disk or disk times an interval has a continuous frame by a finite construction. Take a finite bundle-chart cover and scalar bumps forming a partition of unity, embed fibers complex linearly in $\mathbb C^N$, and form their continuous orthogonal projection $Q=V(V^*V)^{-1}V^*$ in local column matrices. In a star-shaped parametrization of the compact base, uniform continuity provides a finite radial subdivision $x_j=x_0+j(x-x_0)/N_0$ such that $\|Q(x_{j+1})-Q(x_j)\|<1/2$ for every $x,j$. Projection from one image to the next is injective because its change is less than half the input norm; dimensions agree, so it is an isomorphism. The product $Q(x_{N_0})\cdots Q(x_1)$ transports a fixed basis at $x_0$ to a continuous frame everywhere. For a nonzero complex loop define winding by finite local argument lifts; products add winding, reversing orientation negates it, and a continuous homotopy keeps it constant, using uniform continuity and local argument of neighboring ratios. A disk frame change has zero boundary winding because its nonzero determinant contracts radially, so local zero index is frame independent. An orientation-positive source coordinate change also preserves winding: on a sufficiently small circle it deforms to its positive derivative through invertible local coordinates, and a positive linear map deforms to the identity by real Gram–Schmidt, positive rescaling and rotation. Finally, on a Euclidean polygon minus finitely many small round disks, any nonzero complex map has outer winding equal to the sum of its positive hole windings: subdivide by a finite fine grid on which local arguments exist and telescope boundary changes, cancelling interior segments. Grid lines can avoid all circle tangencies and circle-grid vertices because there are finitely many forbidden positions. Thus on each supplied face the winding of a section nonzero on its boundary is the sum of its isolated zero indices inside.

**Construct an auxiliary nonzero section on the entire edge graph times the interval.** At a boundary vertex use the given nonzero section $s$. At every other vertex choose a nonzero continuous path in its line bundle over $[0,1]$, using a frame from step 1.1 and the constant coordinate one. On boundary edges retain the prescribed $s$, which is nonzero there. On an interior edge times the interval use a frame from step 1.1. The two endpoint vertex paths are represented by nonzero functions $a(t),b(t)$. Each has a continuous complex logarithm on $[0,1]$, constructed by finite argument lifts. If $x\in[0,1]$ is the edge coordinate, $\exp((1-x)\log a(t)+x\log b(t))$ is a nonzero section matching both vertices. There are finitely many edges, so these prescriptions define a continuous nonzero section $r$ on the whole one-skeleton times the interval. It agrees with $s$ on the outer boundary. It is not required to agree with either end section on the interior edges. No family of choices indexed by paths or points has been used.

**Compute the invariant from this graph, and compare the actual end sections.** For each face $D$ choose a complex frame on $D\times[0,1]$ by step 1.1. The winding $w_D(r_t)$ along its oriented boundary is constant in $t$, since $r$ is nonzero on that boundary cylinder. At either endpoint $t=0,1$, $s_t$ is nonzero on the graph and the ratio $s_t/r_t$ is therefore a globally defined nonzero complex function there, independent of the local line frame. In each face boundary, product winding gives $w_D(s_t)-w_D(r_t)=w_D(s_t/r_t)$. Sum over faces. On interior edges the ratio is the same and traversed in opposite directions, so its argument changes cancel; on the outer boundary it is one. Thus $\sum_Dw_D(s_t)=\sum_Dw_D(r_t)$. The finite face excision of step 1.1 identifies the left side with the end zero index sum. The right side is constant by its construction. This proves the first assertion even if $s$ has an arbitrary nonisolated intermediate zero set; no transversality or one-manifold trace was required.

**Build the actual normal divisor line.** Use the metric and orientation in the supplied normal disk tube to regard its normal rank-two bundle as a complex line. On the tube $N$ over $Z$, pull this line back by the tube projection and denote its tautological vector at a point of $N$ by $v$. On $W\setminus Z$ use the trivial complex line. Over $N\setminus Z$ glue these bundles by sending a normal vector $\lambda$ to the unique complex scalar $\lambda/v$. This is a smooth nonzero transition function in every complex normal frame, and it is independent of that frame. The sections $v$ and $1$ match under the transition and define a global section $\sigma$ whose zero set is exactly $Z$. Its normal derivative on $Z$ is the identity, with the prescribed normal orientation. Pull back this line and section by $F$. The result satisfies the first assertion on the compact $M\times[0,1]$, and its local end zero index is exactly the stated local intersection number. At a transverse intersection a sufficiently small circle is homotopic through nonzero normal vectors to its invertible derivative image; real positive and negative matrices have degree $+1,-1$, respectively, by the same matrix deformation as in step 1.1. This proves the ordinary geometric intersection assertion.

**Double and then divide by two, with the data kept explicit.** Apply step 4.1 to the supplied doubled problem. Every interior intersection on one copy has a distinct reflected partner of the same local sign or multiplicity by hypothesis. A boundary intersection is fixed and gives the single doubled local intersection stipulated in the data. Hence the doubled total is exactly twice the interior total plus the boundary total, that is $2I$. It is invariant by step 4.1, so $I$ is invariant. This argument establishes the half weight whenever the indicated double is actually supplied; it neither infers a double from a boundary condition alone nor assumes compactness for ends not included in the finite domain.

**Compute the translated branch model completely.** Intersections of the displayed graphs satisfy $w=z+\varepsilon$ and $w^{r+1}=z^{r+1}$. There is no solution with $z=0$. Write $w=\zeta z$, where $\zeta^{r+1}=1$ and $\zeta
e1$. Then $z=\varepsilon/(\zeta-1)$, giving exactly $r$ distinct roots. For $r=0$ the root set is empty. Each root is simple: the complex Jacobian of the two intersection equations has determinant, up to a fixed sign, $(r+1)(w^r-z^r)$, which is nonzero since $w/z=\zeta
e1$ and $\zeta^r=\zeta^{-1}
e1$. The equations are holomorphic in $(w,z)$, so every nonzero complex Jacobian has positive real determinant; each local intersection sign is therefore $+1$. Complex conjugation pairs the nonreal roots because $\varepsilon$ is real. A real root occurs precisely for $\zeta=-1$, hence at most once. Every conjugate pair contributes one root to the upper-half restriction, and each real root has weight one half. The weighted sum is consequently $r/2$. Scaling $\varepsilon$ scales all these roots, so they lie in any prescribed small neighborhood for sufficiently small nonzero translation. This proves the final local assertion with its boundary convention.
